sections.html:
• Common names: Pulse coral, Pumping Xenia, Red Sea Xenia, Pom Pom coral
  • Scientific name: Xenia elongata
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Propagation: easy to moderate
  • Lighting: medium to high
  • Water flow: any (low flow for the pulsing motion)
  • Salinity: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: <0.5 ppm
  • Feeding: photosynthetic
  • Tank placement: low or middle sections
  • Growth rate: fast
  • Toxicity: yes
  • Invasive: yes (potentially)
  • Temper: peaceful
  • Colour forms: pink, tan, grey, cream and white

This coral is hardy, attractive and entertaining, and it doesn't cost much to own one.

Pulsing Xenia makes an interesting addition to established reef tanks. It comes in a variety of colours such as pink, tan, grey, cream and white, and the pulsing motion of the numerous fleshy polyps appeals to viewers. It pairs well with zoas, but excessive growth needs watching, and the population should be reduced when necessary. Rather than keeping a surplus, surplus colonies can be given to other reef hobbyists or sold.

Pulsing Xenia belongs to the family Xeniidae and genus Xenia, which comprises soft corals with fairly large polyps capable of pulsing. It is a hardy, fast-growing coral native to the Indo-Pacific and the Red Sea.

Taxonomy: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Cnidaria, Class Anthozoa, Order Alcyonacea, Family Xeniidae, Genus Xenia, Species Xenia elongata.

This colonial animal naturally lives in shallow waters with mild currents in the Indo-Pacific and the Red Sea. It grows quite fast and is usually found attached to rockwork in the wild.

In captivity, Pulsing Xenia prefers areas with moderate lighting and water movement. There should be plenty of space in the tank for new polyps, since the coral reproduces rapidly in optimal conditions.

It is a colonial coral with multiple individual polyps, often found on a piece of solid substrate such as live rock. Colonies vary in size from a few centimetres to over 50 cm across. The polyps sit on sturdy stalks (5–8 cm long), and each stalk ends in a ring of large, feathery pinnate tentacles, usually eight per polyp. The polyps produce a rhythmic pulsing or pumping action by opening and closing their tentacles.

The role of the pulsing is still unknown, although it is claimed to aid respiration, enhance photosynthetic efficiency, and help with the removal of gases and waste.

Because of its size and growth rate, Pulsing Xenia should be housed in a saltwater tank of at least 40 litres. It may also be kept in smaller nano tanks, provided the coral is placed appropriately and fragged or harvested when due.

Placement. Do not put Pulsing Xenia on the main rock with other corals. Put it on a separate island rock with sand between, which helps keep it from spreading too much. It prefers rocks in the low or middle sections of the tank, where it gets bright light and gentle flow to grow healthily and keep pulsing. It can also serve as nutrient export and be placed in a refugium to scrub excess dissolved nutrients. Aggressive corals (such as Frogspawn or Torch corals) placed around its perimeter will sting it back and prevent expansion.

Care. The main concern is its rapid growth and reproduction, so adequate care is needed to prevent it spreading across the aquarium. Do not keep it with other fast-growing soft corals such as Kenya trees and Green star polyps (GSP will take over Xenia). Monitor growth and prune as the population increases, unless you want the whole reef tank covered with Xenia.

Trimming Xenia is difficult. It is too slippery to grab with fingers, so use tweezers or similar, grab it right at the base and twist it off the rock. It takes a lot of time, and any tissue left on the rock will regrow. Turn off all flow during trimming and do not let any bits float free, because that is how invasions start in the tank.

Growth can also be controlled by reducing nutrients in the water. Xenia is sensitive to pristine water and prefers some nutrients, so do not add a lot of activated carbon. Regular partial water changes replace depleted trace elements vital to the coral's health. Test the water weekly with an accurate test kit and keep parameters at their proper levels. Maintain adequate spacing from neighbouring corals.

Common problems.

  • Grows like a weed: once established, it spreads very fast and is extremely hard to get rid of.
  • Melts away: for unclear reasons Xenia does not grow well in some tanks. Most often it is a lack of nutrients: Pulsing Xenia likes some nitrate, not filthy water. It also does poorly at low pH, especially when moved from a tank with higher pH.
  • Smell: after trimming, do not leave pieces in the rubbish bin; they smell very strongly.
  • Does not pulse: it can have many causes, such as too strong flow, unsuitable water parameters or stress after fragging. For example, soft corals decreased pulsation by around 30% at 32°C compared with 26°C.

• Temperature: 22–26°C
  • pH: 8.1–8.4
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH, for healthy growth and longevity
  • Specific gravity: 1.023–1.025

Soft corals decreased their pulsation by around 30% at 32°C compared with 26°C, according to a study.

Pulsing Xenia requires moderate to high lighting for optimal growth, although it can also do well under low to moderate light. Provide enough bright, indirect light so the coral can photosynthesise with the symbiotic alga (zooxanthellae) living in its tissue. Common lighting for reef tanks with this species is full-spectrum LED, VHO, metal halide and T5; LED seems the most suitable.

Pulsing Xenia is very hardy and can thrive in any water flow, but flow directly affects its pulsation. Too much water movement reduces the pulsing, as strong flow bends the tentacles and can prevent movement altogether. To enjoy the pulsing effect, keep it in low-flow areas.

Like other photosynthetic corals, Pulsing Xenia obtains most of its nutrition through photosynthesis by the symbiotic alga in its tissue. It is also a suspension feeder: it traps planktonic matter with its fleshy, feathery polyps and absorbs nutrients from the water directly through its skin.

Pulsing Xenia has no digestive tract in its stalk. Although the pulsing may look like feeding, it is not.

Whether feeding is needed depends on water quality. If the water contains enough nutrients, feeding may not be necessary, and many aquarists do not feed Pulsing Xenia. Otherwise, it is better to give micro-plankton (bioplankton) from time to time. In the wild, Xenia species have even been found thriving in polluted waters.

In an experiment, glucose enrichment maintained soft coral growth rate by 62% (low), 45% (medium) and 13% (high) compared with controls, indicating that additional energy sources up to a certain threshold may increase the resistance of the corals.

  • Photosynthetic: yes
  • Diet type: micro-plankton
  • Feeding frequency: 1–2 times a week

Pulsing Xenia is a beginner soft coral for established reef aquaria. It is peaceful and reef-compatible, but because of its rapid growth, spread and reproduction it is best kept in a species-only aquarium.

A single Pulsing Xenia can form 10 or more coral heads within a few months, spreading widely over rockwork and growing over sessile animals. This is aided by its strong nutrient absorption from the water through its soft tissue. It will likely outcompete other corals and anemones for nutrients and space, and can take over the whole tank if neglected. Keep a minimum spacing of 15 cm between the Xenia colony and nearby corals.

  • Peaceful: yes
  • Toxicity: no
  • Invasive: yes

Pulsing Xenia reproduces in three ways: sexual reproduction, asexual reproduction and manual fragging.

Sexual reproduction. Gametes are released and fertilised in the water, often forming planula larvae that later develop into polyps.

Asexual reproduction. A parent coral may bud off smaller polyps to form new colonies, often when there is no room left on the rock. This can be used instead of fragging: place another rock next to the colony, wait until the Xenia grows onto it, then remove that rock and repeat. Generally, Xenia does not break off and attach to other rocks if it has space to grow, which is why it has to be trimmed often.

Fragging. Split a healthy mature colony with a sharp blade or scalpel:

  • Locate a stalk and cut it carefully below the stalk, as close to the live rock as possible.
  • Cut it off the main body.
  • Do not glue the freshly cut pieces right away. Pulsing Xenia is a jelly-like soft coral and is hard to attach.
  • Put the piece in a very low-flow or no-flow area so it is not blown away, for 2–3 days. In most cases it attaches to something by then. After that, glue it to a frag plug and return it to the tank.

Alternatively, gently rubber-band the pieces to the frag plug, just enough to hold them down.

Items you might need depending on the method: hammer and chisel, scissors, cyanoacrylate glue, containers, scalpel or razor blade, plug pebbles or coral frag discs.
